messages:
mira: Quick sync — thinking out loud about a long-term refactor for our canary / A-B routing + automatic fallback. Current problem: routing and observer both hold bits of rollout state and it leaks complexity into the placement layer.

alex: +1. Can you summarize the main pain points?

mira: Sure. 1) Routing needs to decide per-request which variant to hit, but it also sometimes judges observability signals (e.g. sudden p95 jump) and starts short-circuiting. 2) Observer owns telemetry windows and decides when to mark a variant unhealthy. 3) We have ad-hoc RPCs between them for trial rollbacks. This causes racey decisions and unclear ownership during transient events.

jon: We've seen that cause double-rollbacks where both the router and the observer flip flags and they fight each other for 30s. Not great for client latencies.

lee: Proposed pattern: a single "canary arbitrator" service that owns the policy evaluation and exposes a simple routing API. Router becomes stateless and only asks arbitrator: "shouldRoute(requestCtx, variantId) -> allow|deny|slow-path". Observer streams signals to arbitrator.

mira: Exactly. Arbitrator would expose lightweight decision endpoints and a subscription stream for soft signals. It would also keep a short-lived timeline of decisions to make post-hoc analysis easier.

sara: How do we avoid making the arbitrator another bottleneck?

alex: We make it hierarchical: local arbitrators per region/node-group (fast, caches decisions), with a central coordinator for global rollouts. Local arbitrators evaluate most requests from cached policies and recent probe telemetry. Central coordinator handles policy changes, long-window aggregates, and cross-tenant signals.

mira: Also propose a "soft-switch" grace period concept: when a variant is toggled to degrade, the arbitrary doesn't instantly drop traffic. Instead it moves to a slow-path for N seconds where router applies sampling/backoff before full cutover. This limits thrash and gives time for probes to converge.

jon: I like slow-path. Can we express it as a configurable policy block? Example config:

```yaml
canary_policy:
  warmup_seconds: 120
  slowpath_seconds: 30
  warmup_fraction: 0.1
  telemetry_windows: [60, 300]
  rollback_thresholds:
    p95_latency_ms: 2000
    error_rate: 0.02
```

lee: Nice. Implementation note: routers will implement three modes per-variant: OPEN, SLOWPATH, CLOSED. SLOWPATH semantics are local: e.g. drop 80% of new sessions or serve them via fallback model.

sara: What's the interface for observer -> arbitrator? Push only, or pull?

mira: Push for immediate probes (heartbeats, canary-specific probes). Pull for long aggregates. We'll use a gRPC stream for probe pushes and a REST reconcile for pulls/rollup.

alex: Failure modes: if arbitrator is unreachable, routers should default to conservative behavior — route to baseline variant and mark event in trace. No automatic traffic to new variants if arbitrator unreachable.

deploy-bot: deploy: canary-arbitrator: staging -> cluster-a at 2024-11-03T17:12Z :rocket:

jon: One more operational requirement: expose a simple debug endpoint that returns the last 60s of decisions and probes for a given variant (for oncall). Keep it redactable for PII.

lee: For rollout policy language, keep it limited: time windows, slowpath semantics, thresholds, and optional external gating flags (compliance, infra). No arbitrary scripts.

mira: Next steps: I can draft an RFC capturing: interface surface (grpc decision + stream ingest + REST management), data model for telemetry windows, retries/backoff, and a small PoC local arbitrator that just proxies decisions from a central coordinator with caching. Anyone wants to co-author?

alex: I can take the data model section. jon will own failure-mode tests. lee can sketch the router change PR. sara will write operational runbook hooks.

mira: Perfect. I'll write the RFC draft this week and ping owners. Thanks all :) :thumbsup:
